extracted.intended_audience: company management, investor relations teams, underwriters, and employees preparing for an IPO or quarterly earnings communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for corporate insiders and investor-relations teams on what communications are permitted or restricted during quiet periods for IPOs, financings, and quarterly earnings. Covers timelines, examples of violations, social media risks, and when to consult legal/advisory counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit insider public communications during quiet periods
rubrics_metrics.description: A quiet period is the period of time when company insiders are required to limit certain business-related communication with the public. During this time, communication is monitored and enforced by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Quiet period guidelines apply to private companies throughout their IPO process and publicly traded companies during the weeks leading up to their quarterly earnings calls and when they are issuing securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to avoid selective disclosure of material non-public information and prevent an artificial increase in demand before companies issue securities. Management, employees, and underwriters should treat communications conservatively during these windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPO timeline: waiting period and post-pricing quiet phase
rubrics_metrics.description: For private companies issuing public shares for the first time (IPO), the quiet period begins once management and the underwriters reach an agreement and file a registration statement (S-1) with the SEC. Once the S-1 becomes publicly available, the 'waiting period' starts and ends on the day the price is set for the issued securities. After pricing, the company enters a final phase of the quiet period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final post-pricing phase aims to allow stock to trade without influence from new information; its length is determined by underwriting banks and can last anywhere from 10–25 days. Be aware of each phase's start/end triggers (filing, public S-1, pricing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'gun-jumping' before and during IPO process
rubrics_metrics.description: During the time the registration remains confidential at the SEC, any hint of an imminent IPO by the filing company or underwriter can be considered 'gun-jumping.' Although this term is not formally defined, it includes any action taken by the company or underwriters that may improperly stimulate demand for the IPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common historical gun-jumping communications: formal investor meetings, press releases, and interviews. Modern examples also include social media posts, unusual website updates, and spontaneous increases in advertising. Consequences include delays to IPO timelines (cooling-off periods), fines, and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: During the waiting period management should avoid interviews and hyping demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the S-1 is public, management teams should remain cautious and avoid giving interviews. This will prevent hyping up demand before pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the final two weeks, management may meet potential investors on a roadshow but must not disclose information not in the S-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-pricing communications must be limited to S-1 disclosures; amendments required for new information
rubrics_metrics.description: In the post-pricing quiet period, conversations with investors are limited to contents in the S-1. Saying anything outside of what’s disclosed in the S-1 during this time will require an amended version to be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sell-side analysts from underwriting banks are also restricted from issuing research reports on the company during this time. Be mindful that introducing new substantive information requires regulatory amendment and disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party materials and social media sharing can constitute violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing third-party materials can also be considered a violation. This applies to sharing on company-related social media accounts and employees’ personal accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must control both official channels and employee conduct online; even indirect or third-party content can trigger gun-jumping concerns. Apply conservative social-media policies during sensitive periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarterly quiet periods for public companies are aimed at avoiding selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For publicly traded companies, the quiet period refers to the time between the end of a financial quarter and the company announcing financial results. The goal remains the same: avoid selective disclosure of material information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining when to begin the quarterly quiet period depends on when finance and accounting have finalized or nearly finalized quarterly results and management has a reliable sense of performance. The formal quarter-end quiet period begins at quarter close and extends until the company’s earnings call, though some teams include days leading up to quarter close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan investor events around quiet periods—prefer post-earnings timing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to take your quiet period into consideration when planning non-deal roadshows or scheduling investor calls because management will be limited in the information they can share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investor events are much more productive when hosted shortly after an earnings call because management has more leeway to answer investor questions. Schedule roadshows and investor communication to avoid constrained periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, err on the side of caution and consult advisors/counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to the increased scrutiny companies are held to during an IPO, it is highly recommended that you consult with your IPO advisory firm and legal counsel regarding requests for interviews, quotes, meetings, as well as social media posts and press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples (Salesforce, Webvan) show that public-facing commentary close to IPO can trigger SEC scrutiny and negotiated remedies (e.g., cooling-off periods). Use legal/advisory review for borderline communications and establish internal approval workflows during quiet periods.
